items.title: AppleInsider favorite 'Oxygen Not Included' is now Apple SIlicon native
items.content_html: In a quality of life update, Klei has finally added Apple Silicon native code to the long-running and AppleInsider-favorite base-building game. The game was pretty fast with Rosetta before, but paired with that and some new memory optimizations, the game is speedy now on even older Apple Silicon Macs!

Nvidia's chip smuggling scandal goes deeper than Jensen Huang
items.content_html:
Nvidia's leadership can't catch a break, as another executive has been dragged into a $2.5 billion chip smuggling scandal while former CEO Jensen Huang prepares for a visit to the U.S. Senate.

The major news surrounding Nvidia has centered around former CEO Jensen Huang and his extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. However, it seems the executive rot goes a little bit further into the company's leadership.

Cenly Chen has been accused of smuggling $2.5 billion worth of chips into China, reports The Telegraph. Chen, who previously worked at SuperMicro as chief growth officer, is married to former Nvidia executive vice president of field operations, Jay Puri.

Puri retired from his role in July, in a seemingly unconnected move.

The SuperMicro scandal erupted earlier in 2026, after co-founder Wally Liaw was charged by the U.S. government for sending Nvidia chips to China via Taiwan. Liaw has pleaded not guilty.

Curved glass edges of iPhone 20 will be practically invisible from the front
items.content_html:
The curved glass elements of the iPhone 20 could be just a millimeter thick, a leaker adds to their previous claims about the anniversary model.

On Tuesday, serial leaker Ice Universe posted a video to X, seemingly showing off what they thought was the curved glass of the iPhone 20 Pro. One day later, the leaker added a bit of extra information about the inbound models.

Posting to Weibo on Wednesday, Ice Universe claims Apple is working on four models. Two allegedly use flat glass covers, while two will have curved glass.

The curved glass has also been prototyped for three years and underwent several revisions, they add. This isn't exactly new information, as Apple's patent filings have discussed the advantages of curved glass enclosures for far longer than that.

The leaker continues, insisting that the curved bezels of the glass are approximately 1mm deep. This seems plausible if the previous video truly is from an Apple supplier working on the glass and not an accessory producer prototyping screen protectors.

Those bezels will apparently be close to invisible to users when viewed from the front. The result will be something close to a borderless design.

The size of the bezels are also seemingly not as extreme as what Apple previously intended. Ice Universe says that the earliest version had a very large curvature, which was later reduced.

They conclude their post by saying that the industry is optimistic about the curved design versus the foldable iPhone Duo.

Generally speaking, Weibo leakers aren't known for their accuracy, due to regurgitating rumors from elsewhere with little in the way of fact-checking. Ice Universe does have a reasonably good track record among Weibo leakers, but it should still be taken with caution.

Ice Universe's posts continue a line of claims about the glass of the anniversary model, such as using a glass assembly similar to the iPhone Air. The curved glass has also been claimed to create a bezel-less effect, thanks to optical refraction.

There has also been claims that Apple will use a quad-curved OLED display for the Pro model.

items.title: Phishing scams get a new watchdog as Moonlock expands to iPhone
items.content_html:
MacPaw is bringing Moonlock to the iPhone, giving users tools to spot phishing scams and check their security settings without relying on traditional antivirus software.

The iPhone app centers on Scam Detect, which analyzes content that users paste, scan or share with Moonlock. Rather than flagging something as suspicious, it explains what might be wrong, including links that don't match the sender they're supposed to represent.

Users can send content to Moonlock directly from other apps through the iOS share sheet. The QR code scanner also lets them inspect a destination before opening it, which could help with scams that hide fraudulent websites behind seemingly ordinary codes.

Moonlock's Safe SMS feature takes a more automatic approach. When enabled in iPhone Settings, it filters suspected scam messages from unknown senders into the Junk folder in Messages and explains why each message was flagged.

The filter only checks new texts from unknown senders, so it won't examine existing conversations or older messages. Users can still review anything it catches, and Moonlock doesn't delete the filtered texts.

MacPaw's Email Breach History feature checks up to five email addresses against known data breaches. If it finds a match, Moonlock identifies the affected service, when the breach happened and what information was exposed, then helps users secure their accounts.

A separate Security Score rates an iPhone's configuration on a scale from zero to 100. Moonlock checks Wi-Fi security, passcode protection, iOS updates and signs of jailbreaking, then recommends changes users can make to improve their score.

Moonlock for iPhone isn't the same as its Mac counterpart

MacPaw launched Moonlock for macOS in October 2025 with real-time malware protection, scheduled scans, network monitoring and a built-in VPN. The iPhone version doesn't include those antivirus capabilities.

Apple's security restrictions prevent third-party iPhone apps from scanning other apps and their files for malware. MacPaw has instead focused on detecting scams and helping people understand the protections already available on their devices.

There's some overlap with Apple's existing tools. The iPhone already supports message filtering for unknown senders, and third-party extensions can identify suspected spam without requiring a separate security app.

Apple's Passwords app also warns you when a login you've saved turns up in a known data leak.

Apple's Passwords app also warns you when a login you've saved turns up in a known data leak. Moonlock checks your email addresses against reported breaches, even if you haven't saved the affected logins in Passwords.

Moonlock's main advantage is bringing those checks together with tools for examining suspicious content. Whether that makes it more effective at catching scams is another question, particularly when some of its detection features involve sending information to outside services.

According to MacPaw's privacy disclosures, Safe SMS initially analyzes incoming messages on the iPhone. If its local model can't confidently classify a text, the message may be sent through MacPaw's servers to OpenAI for further analysis.

Content submitted through Scam Detect is also processed by OpenAI. MacPaw says it doesn't store SMS content on its own servers, although OpenAI may retain submitted information for up to 30 days for abuse monitoring without using it to train models.

If you use Moonlock to check for scams, you're letting the app examine your private communications. MacPaw's launch announcement didn't include independent detection benchmarks or false-positive rates, so it's hard to judge how reliably Moonlock catches scams or how often it flags legitimate messages.

Moonlock for iPhone arrives November 18, 2026, through the App Store and Setapp. The App Store lists a seven-day free trial, followed by subscriptions costing $9.99 per month or $49.99 annually, and the app requires iOS 26 or later.

Existing Setapp subscribers won't need a separate iPhone purchase. MacPaw says one Moonlock subscription through Setapp covers both Mac and iPhone without requiring another account.
